Pursuant to Regulation 34(1) and 53(2) of the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) 
Regulations, 2015 ( “Listing Regulations” ), as amended from time to time, please find enclosed herewith 
the Integrated  Annual  Report including  the Annual Accounts  and the Business Responsibility and 
Sustainability Report  (“BRSR” ) for the Financial Year 202 5-26 (“Annual Report” ) along with the AGM Notice 
being sent to all Members in electronic mode.  
 
With a vision focused on the future, Vedanta is transforming into a global natural resources, energy and 
technology leader. As India accelerates towards a new era of growth, Vedanta 2.0 is building the 
foundations of tomorrow through critical minerals, ene rgy, technology and world -class resources. By 
expanding capacity, embracing innovation and advancing sustainability, we are powering growth, enabling 
progress and creating enduring value for all stakeholders. Driven by operational excellence and a 
commitme nt to nation -building, we are shaping a stronger, more resilient and sustainable future for 
generations to come.

for gaining insight into the Company’s performance:

2. Sustainability Report  
3. Climate Action Report

=== page 24 ===
Vedanta Limited, a 
subsidiary of Vedanta Resources Limited, is a global natural resources conglomerate. Our strategic asset base across India, Africa and the Middle East positions us to serve growing global demand. We operate across zinc-lead-silver, iron ore, steel, copper, aluminium, power, nickel, and oil and gas, holding market-leading positions in several of these businesses. 
Integrated reporting
Integrated Reporting explains 
how we create, preserve and, where relevant, erode value over time, aligned with our purpose, strategy and values. Since adopting Integrated Reporting in FY 2017-18, we have strengthened integrated thinking and continuously enhanced our disclosures.
The FY 2025-26 report presents 
a comprehensive view of our material matters, their impact on the environment and society, and the associated risks and opportunities influencing business performance. It supports an informed assessment of our ability to create value across the short, medium and long term.Scope and boundary
The Integrated Report and Annual Accounts 2025-26 cover the reporting period from 01 April 2025 to 31 March 2026 and provides a comprehensive overview of Vedanta Limited (Vedanta, VEDL), a subsidiary of Vedanta Resources Limited.
It reflects performance across our 
business segments: zinc-lead-silver, oil and gas, aluminium, power, iron ore, steel, nickel and copper. Our assets span India, South Africa and the Middle East, covering the full value chain from exploration and asset development to extraction, processing and value-addition.
The report explains our performance, 
strategy and value creation model through an interlinked multi-capital framework. It also outlines stakeholder engagement practices, governance structures and risk management processes.
Approach to stakeholder 
engagement and materiality
Our stakeholders include individuals 
and organisations whose interests or actions influence our ability to execute strategy and sustain performance. We engage regularly with key stakeholder groups to understand expectations and address concerns.
This report focusses on material matters 
that affect our capacity to create value over the short, medium and long term.
Annual accounts
This report should be read alongside 
the Annual Accounts (pages 428 to 725) for a complete understanding of VEDL ’s financial performance.
The consolidated and standalone 
financial statements have been prepared in accordance with Indian Accounting Standards (Ind AS) notified under the Companies (Indian Accounting Standards) Rules, 2015, as amended. These statements have been independently audited by S.R. Batliboi & Co. LLP . The Independent Auditors’ Reports for consolidated and standalone financial statements appear on pages 428 and 725 respectively.Board and management assurance
The Board of Directors and the Company’s management accept responsibility for the integrity and completeness of information presented in this report. To the best of their knowledge, the report addresses all material matters and fairly represents the integrated performance, position and impacts of Vedanta Limited.
Forward-looking statements
This report contains ‘forward-looking statements’ – that is, statements about business expectations and forecasts that are based on future, not past events. In this context, forward-looking statements address our expected future business and financial performance, and often contain words such as ‘expects’, ‘anticipates’, ‘intends’, ‘plans’, ‘believes’, ‘seeks’, or ‘will’. Forward-looking statements by their nature address matters that are, in different degrees, uncertain. For us, uncertainties arise from the behaviour of financial and metals markets including the London Metal Exchange, fluctuations in interest and/or exchange rates and metal prices; from future integration of acquired businesses; and from numerous other matters of national, regional and global scale, including those of environmental, climatic, natural, political, economic, business, competitive or regulatory nature. These uncertainties may cause our actual future results to be materially different than those expressed in our forward-looking statements. We do not undertake to update our forward-looking statements. These forward-looking statements involve risk and uncertainties, and although we believe that the assumption on which our forward-looking statements are based are reasonable, any of those assumptions could prove to be inaccurate and, as a result, the forward-looking statement based on those assumptions could be materially incorrect.Information coverage:

Integrated thinking at Vedanta 
Vision behind
THE TRANSITION
Integrated thinking remains central to how Vedanta evolves and creates long-term value by combining financial 
performance and operational excellence with ESG priorities, stakeholder interests and emerging market opportunities. It informs our strategic choices, including our transition to Vedanta 2.0. Through this strategic transformation, we are repositioning our portfolio aligned with India’s needs in energy transition, critical minerals, advanced manufacturing, and clean technologies, while harnessing AI, automation, and innovation to drive agility and future-readiness. Our ‘Transforming for Good’ ESG framework remains a guiding force. Embedded across operations, it supports responsible growth, disciplined risk management and strengthens business resilience.

Vedanta at a Glance
Vedanta Limited, a subsidiary of Vedanta 
Resources Limited, is a global natural resources conglomerate with a diversified portfolio spanning zinc-lead-silver, iron ore, steel, copper, aluminium, power, nickel, and oil and gas. Our strategic, tier-1 asset base across India, Africa and the Middle East positions us to serve growing global demand.
With the world around us changing, we are 
building for the future by embarking on a strategic transformation to Vedanta 2.0. We are moving beyond traditional minerals to integrate high-potential critical minerals with a focus on energy transition and clean energy, aiming to reshape 70% of our portfolio. We are investing in artificial intelligence-driven systems, automation and innovation to ensure the next phase of growth is smarter, more efficient and value accretive.
At Vedanta, we are building a foundation 
for India's clean energy future, where access to critical minerals supports innovation, economic growth, and global competitiveness. As we do so, we continue to be guided by our ESG leadership to ensure that India's critical resources are harnessed responsibly, while empowering communities and delivering enduring value for all stakeholders.The one

scale of transformation demands we rise 
even higher. That is the genesis of Vedanta 2.0 – to be a global leader in critical minerals, energy, and technology, while creating long-term value for our shareholders, communities, and the planet.
Vedanta 2.0: Where We Stand
The demerger of Vedanta into five independent, pure-play entities is complete. All four resulting entities are now listed and trading on the exchanges along with the flagship Vedanta Limited. Each business has been structurally fortified with independent focus, sharper strategy, and stronger capital structures to independently unlock shareholder value and compete with the best in the world.
Scale is central to Vedanta 2.0. and 
FY 2025-26 marked a breakthrough year. We successfully commissioned major expansion projects across aluminium, zinc, oil & gas, and power, with a capex spend of over ₹ 15,000 crore. We have ₹ 17,000–19,000 crore earmarked for growth capex in FY 2026-27. Zinc India's Board has separately approved Phase I capex of ~₹ 17,000 crore to expand refined metal capacity from 1.14 to 2 million metric tonnes. Our total capex outlay now stands at ~US$ 8 billion, of which ~US$ 4 billion has already been deployed as of 31 March 2026.
We are also reshaping our portfolio for the 
future. We have secured 3 new strategic mineral blocks, taking our total critical mineral composite licences to 10, spanning copper, nickel, chromium, cobalt, vanadium, potash, manganese, tungsten, gold, and rare earth elements. Resource security through domestic processing is not optional for India. It is imperative. And we are leading the charge.The path forward is full of promise as we have demerged into pure-play businesses with each capable of becoming a Vedanta in its own right. There is no shortage of opportunity.
Vedanta 2.0: Built for a Changing World
We are living through a defining moment in human history. Energy transition, technological advancement, and AI reshaping global priorities. As the fastest growing major economy in the world, India is pivotal in this new world. For us, rapid industrialisation, large-scale infrastructure build-up, an AI and digital-driven economy, and exponential energy demand are all converging at once.
This entire economy is underwritten by 
minerals, metals and energy. To cut imports, tomorrow's India will need far greater investments in these sectors. And Vedanta is perfectly positioned and ready.
Our portfolio spanning 15 major 
commodities, oil & gas, and 5 GW of merchant power capacity makes us strategically vital to India's progress. But the

A NEW ERA OF GROWTH
I have spent most of my

Commodity prices have witnessed 
significant volatility in recent quarters. What safeguards are in place to sustain performance and protect margins?
The commodity markets have always been cyclical. 
What distinguishes the current environment is 
the scale, frequency and multi-variable nature of volatility. Prices are witnessing sharp swings in a matter of days. In our experience, this is one of the most complex markets to navigate.
Vedanta’s resilience stems from diversification, 
vertical integration and domestic demand exposure. Our portfolio spans 15+ commodities, which are primarily consumed within India, providing resilience against global uncertainty. Our backward integration and cost leadership further reduce vulnerability to price volatility.
Our disciplined approach to hedging provides 
cashflow certainty, downside protection against volatility, while retaining meaningful exposure to favourable pricing.
Can you walk us through the key operational 
and financial highlights across Vedanta’s core businesses during the year?
FY 2025-26 was marked by broad-based 
performance across all major verticals. Key highlights of the performance include:
Aluminium
The business attained the highest-ever production 
for alumina as well as aluminium. Alumina volumes rose by 48% to 2,916 kt, while that of aluminium by 1% to 2,456 kt. Hot metal cost at US$ 1,752/t was the lowest in the last 5 years, while VAP output increased to 60% of aluminium production. This helped achieve the best-ever quarterly and yearly EBITDA margins at 1,512 US$/t in Q4FY 2025-26 and 1,154 US$/t in FY 2025-26. Under our Green product initiative, this year, we sold the highest-ever volume of low carbon Aluminium at ~91 kt.
Zinc India
Zinc India recorded the highest-ever mined metal 
at 1,114 kt and while refined metal production stood at 1,048 kt, respectively. The business strengthened its global cost leadership through cost reduction and operational optimisation measures. As a result, refined metal production costs reduced by 9% to US$ 959/t, which is the lowest in five years. Saleable silver production stood at 627 t, and together with 75% higher average silver prices, contributed more than 40% to Zinc India’s profits.Q

CASE STUDY
As part of our endeavour to 
be an ESG-forward operator in maritime logistics, we launched Project Uday at our Iron Ore operations in Goa. The project involves installing solar auxiliary power systems on barges to support cleaner onboard energy use. It reduces dependence on diesel-based generation for routine auxiliary loads, improves energy efficiency, lowers emissions and enhances the reliability of essential onboard systems.
The solar system installed on motor 
vessel Mogri helps reduce around 6.5 tonnes of carbon emissions every year, equivalent to nearly 297 trees planted per bargeImpact statementPowering Marine 
Logistics with RenewablesOur approach

CASE STUDY
We are advancing offshore 
blocks across India’s East and West coasts to accelerate production from domestic offshore reserves. At the Ambe block, we adopted lightweight Conductor Supported Platform technology, supported by early engineering and financial commitment, integrated cross-functional execution, phased development planning, and readiness of pipelines and surface facilities.
The Ambe offshore asset is a marginal 
field that requires a capital-efficient development approach to ensure commercial viability. Conventional offshore solutions involve higher capex, longer timelines and larger offshore scope, creating the need for an innovative, fit-for-purpose strategy that can optimise project economics and accelerate installation.Problem statementOur approach
 Adopted a fit-for-purpose offshore development approach built around the principle of ‘design one, build many’
 Evaluated multiple development concepts before selecting the Conductor Supported Platform as the optimal solution for the Ambe marginal field
 Established a strategic partnership with 2H Offshore for end-to-end platform delivery, covering design, engineering, fabrication and installation
 Used CSP technology, where well conductors act as structural support for the topsides, removing the need for conventional heavy jackets
 Retained dry-tree well capability while simplifying offshore infrastructure
 Reduced structural complexity, installation duration and offshore construction scope to enable faster, more efficient execution
 Retained the exploratory well as a keeper well, improving project economics and supporting faster monetisation
 Enabled around 30% reduction in platform capex, accelerated first production timelines and improved project IRRAccelerating

Vedanta response
Vedanta takes pride in being 
innovation-led and technology-driven, integrating advanced technologies to enhance the value of existing assets and drive operational efficiency.
We are utilising drone-based 
surveillance technology across applications in open-cast and underground mining operations.Operational technologies and analytical tools are revolutionising decision-making in the mining industry, driving a paradigm change in functions like mining, smelting as well as power plant operations. These technologies enable digital replication of assets, facilitating visualisation and strategic simulation, optimising decisions on investments and processes. This innovative approach, supported by accessible simulation software, maximises value from existing assets.
Driving Digitally Integrated Operations
This includes successful implementation of Digital Twin which allows us to create a virtual model of critical assets, facilitating simulation and optimisation of operations. This helps enhance our operational processes with highest safety standards.T5

Our risk framework balances materiality and defined risk tolerance levels to provide reasonable assurance against significant 
losses. A structured and consistent process enables clear identification, assessment and reporting of risks to the Board. 
Established management systems, operating processes and strong ethical standards guide the way risks are monitored and 
addressed across the organisation.

Potential impact on the Group
Mining operations generate waste that can cause injuries, loss of life, environmental damage and production disruptions. Tailings dam failure, although rare, remains a critical risk with significant financial and reputational consequences.

Accountability and continuous improvement

Enhanced standards and procedures
 Strengthened standards through annual independent reviews and half-yearly CEO signoffs confirming adherence to design parameters
 Transition to dry tailings facilities where feasible
 Regular training for dam management personnel delivered by third-party experts and international consultants

Defining what matters for lasting impact
Sustained business performance and responsible operations are two sides of the same commitment. In 
FY 2025-26, we conducted our Double Materiality Assessment through an independently facilitated process, engaging approximately 1,600 internal and external stakeholders across surveys, interviews, focussed group discussions, and 14 site visits. The assessment examined 26 material topics through two lenses:
Financial materiality: Considering how sustainability issues affect our business performance and capital.
Impact materiality: Considering how our operations affect people, ecosystems, and economies.
The results directly shape how we allocate resources, set targets, and strengthen disclosures across our 
Transforming for Good  framework. A clearer understanding of which topics carry the highest financial and 
impact significance enables us to manage emerging risks proactively, respond to evolving stakeholder expectations, and pursue opportunities that create lasting value for our business and the communities we serve.Double Materiality Assessment
Focussing on 
WHAT MATTERS FOR THE FUTUREPurpose of Double Materiality 
Assessment (DMA)
We conduct a detailed materiality 
assessment every two years, with an annual management review, to identify and prioritise the topics that matter most to our stakeholders and our business. Our previous assessment was conducted in FY 2022-23, guided by GRI Standards 2021. Building on that foundation, our FY 2025-26 exercise was independently facilitated and aligned with the principles of the EU Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) and leading sector standards, including GRI, ICMM, and SASB, and evaluated positive and negative impacts, risks, and opportunities associated with each of our 26 material topics. The findings inform how we set targets, allocate resources, and strengthen disclosures across the Vedanta Group. Additionally, the key KPIs for our material topics are aligned with annual independent assurance and audit requirements, ensuring we consistently meet our own standards and relevant industry benchmarks. The findings enable us to align our reporting with evolving stakeholder expectations, integrate material ESG risks into our enterprise risk management processes, and reinforce our commitment to long-term value creation and responsible business performance across the Vedanta Group.
Materiality determination 
process
Our approach to materiality determination 
examines each topic through the lens of strategy, risk, capital, and global sustainability priorities to ensure that what we disclose and manage genuinely what matters most. By integrating these elements, we aim to deliver long-term value for our stakeholders while contributing to broader societal and environmental goals and ensuring alignment with the UN Sustainable Development Goals. For each of our 26 material topics, we ensured that our sustainability commitments remain focussed, resilient, and accountable across the Vedanta Group.Identify potential material topics by analysing company disclosures and benchmarking against peer reports, global standards (including GRI 11, GRI 14, ICMM, and SASB), rating methodologies, and expert inputs, followed by consolidation of these insights to develop a mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive list of ESG topics.
1 Identification of potential material topics
Engage key internal and external stakeholders through surveys, interviews, and focussed discussions to validate and prioritise IROs. Over 1,625 internal and external stakeholders were consulted, and inputs were scored to assess impact significance (scope, scale, likelihood, irremediability) and financial risks and opportunities (magnitude and likelihood).3 Stakeholder engagement
Review and validate the materiality outcomes with senior leadership, followed by final approval from the Board-level ESG Committee. The overall process and results were also subjected to independent third-party assurance to ensure transparency and credibility.5 Validation and reviewIdentify and map positive and negative impacts, and financial risks and opportunities for each material topic using internal sources (risk registers, human rights and community assessments) and external inputs (peer reports, media, GRI, SASB, and rating methodologies). This resulted in 250+ IROs, with key risks further assessed for potential financial impact.2 Map Impacts, Risks, and Opportunities (IRO)
Score material topics based on stakeholder inputs and apply weightings for stakeholder influence and interest, along with revenue-based weightages to derive group-level prioritisation, resulting in a consolidated materiality matrix across financial and impact dimensions.4 Development of materiality matrixApproach and methodology 
Our Double Materiality Assessment followed a structured methodology, independently facilitated and informed by leading international frameworks. We analysed both dimensions of materiality, systematically examining how sustainability issues affect our business and how our business affects the world around it across the full breadth of our operations and stakeholder universe.

The natural resources we extract from the ground are essential to economic development. Managing that 
extraction responsibly is fundamental to our own long-term sustainability. Our Transforming for Good strategy is the structured, time-bound expression of that responsibility, organised around three pillars and nine Aims that translate our sustainability commitments into measurable actions across the communities we operate within, the ecosystems we depend on, and the workplaces we are responsible for.Our ESG Commitment
Transforming together for a 
SUSTAINABLE FUTURE  Our overarching objective is to 
generate lasting value for all stakeholders while managing our operations in an environmentally responsible, socially inclusive, and governance-compliant manner. Transforming Communities keeps the welfare of people and local communities at the centre of our business decisions. Transforming the Planet embeds environmental responsibility into how we operate, invest, and grow. Transforming the Workplace builds a safe, inclusive, and well-governed organisation where every individual can thrive.
Each Aim is anchored by specific, 
time-bound targets and KPIs that are tracked, reported, and progressively aligned for independent assurance. Our governance architecture, from the Board ESG Committee through to site-level Communities of Practice, ensures that progress is monitored with the same rigour we apply to financial performance.As Vedanta enters a period of strategic evolution, with sector-focussed demergers sharpening the accountability and operational focus of each business, our Transforming for Good framework provides the shared sustainability architecture that binds our portfolio together. Each business shares the same commitment to grow in ways that strengthen communities, restore natural systems, and build workplaces where people thrive.

=== page 77 ===
Vedanta plays a foundational role in India’s development story, as one of the country’s most significant 
producers of critical natural resources and a company whose operations span energy, metals, mining, and technology at a national scale. Over six decades, this presence has been shaped by a conviction that industrial scale and responsible conduct are not competing priorities but mutually reinforcing ones. With a steadfast commitment to sustainability, ethical governance, and community stewardship, Vedanta integrates ESG principles into the architecture of its operations, aligning with global benchmarks and contributing to India’s progress toward self-reliance, inclusive prosperity, and long-term resilience.Our ESG Strategy
Where ambition 
MEETS ACCOUNTABILITYOur philosophy, ‘Building on Legacy, 
Synergising Value, Scaling Impact’, 
captures the moment Vedanta is in. It is a company that honours its foundation while transforming its structure: strategic demergers are creating focussed, sector leading entities with dedicated capital and sharper accountability, each empowered to meet global sustainability expectations with greater precision. ESG is not a framework applied to the business. It is the framework within which every strategic decision is made, from how we govern tailings and decarbonise operations, to how we invest in communities and build the workforce of the future. The ambition is clear. The accountability is by design.
This evolution empowers each 
independent entity to meet specific global sustainability expectations with greater precision, while carrying forward the standards, targets, and accountability mechanisms that bind our portfolio together. Our ESG commitments travel with each business unchanged.
The challenges we face, from 
climate change and water security to biodiversity, social inclusion, human rights, and governance, require integrated responses embedded at every level of the organisation. Our framework addresses these through three strategic pillars: Transforming Communities, which focusses on empowering 2.5 million families through education, healthcare, and skills; Transforming the Planet, which targets a 25% reduction in our carbon footprint and integration of 2.5 GW of renewable energy RTC; and Transforming the Workplace, which advances workforce safety, health, and inclusive diversity across our operations.
Capability building
Building internal capability is central to this effort. Through the Vedanta Academy for Sustainability (VEDAS), we equip our employees and partners to embed ESG principles into everyday business decisions, ensuring our sustainability commitments translate into operational reality across all sites and functions.Monitoring progress
Progress is tracked through a 
combination of mechanisms, with the ESG Scorecard serving as a core tool rather than the sole measure. The Scorecard monitors each Aim through time-bound KPIs with defined baselines and short-, medium-, and long-term targets to FY 2029-30. This is complemented by regular operational reviews, real-time implementation tracking, and continuous feedback loops embedded across business units.Performance is reviewed monthly by the ESG Executive Committee and reported biannually to the Board, with ESG parameters carrying a 15% weighting in leadership performance linked KPIs. The governance framework emphasises transparency, leadership accountability, and alignment with BRSR, GRI, TCFD, TNFD, and SASB standards, alongside active engagement with investors, regulators, communities, and employees to ensure strategies deliver measurable and shared value.VEDAS: GROWING A SUSTAINABILITY-
LITERATE ORGANISATION
Launched in February 2025, 
the Vedanta Academy for Sustainability (VEDAS) embeds ESG capability across every function and level of the organisation. It is built on a simple premise: sustainability is integral to all business decisions, not a standalone function.
Through a science-led, action-
oriented curriculum aligned with Vedanta’s operations, VEDAS enables employees to evaluate everyday decisions through an ESG lens, integrating risk, compliance, resource efficiency, and long-term resilience into core processes.
Structured along an 
“Understand, Act, Lead”  
pathway, the programme reached around 7,000 executive employees at the Foundation level in FY 2025-26, establishing a common baseline in sustainability fundamentals. Ongoing engagement mechanisms, including the VEDAS Monthly Quiz, help build a network of Business Unit Ambassadors.
The Champion Programme 
forms the leadership tier, converting engaged employees into action-oriented leaders who drive on ground implementation through community linked missions. Looking ahead, VEDAS will scale to over 25,000 learners, expand to include the social dimension of ESG, and introduce a dedicated Sustainability Month. By FY 2029-30, it aims to reach over 1,00,000 employees and partners, embedding sustainability-led decision-makingacross Vedanta’s operations.

ESG GOVERNANCE
Accountability by design, not by declaration
Our ESG governance architecture clearly distributes accountability across four interlocking levels while preserving the agility 
to respond to an evolving ESG landscape.
The defining feature of this architecture is its two-directional flow. Strategy, standards, and direction move downward from the 
Board. Performance intelligence, operational learning, and ground-level innovation move upward through our 13 Communities of Practice. Neither direction functions without the other. The quality of that two-way exchange is what determines whether our ESG commitments translate into measurable outcomes.

A multi-tiered framework for 
accountability
Our ESG governance operates 
through interlocking levels, each with a defined remit, cadence, and set of decision rights. No level operates in isolation; each one feeds into and draws from the levels adjacent to it.
Board ESG committee: 
Strategic oversight
The Board ESG Committee is 
the apex accountability body for Vedanta's sustainability performance. It sets strategic direction, reviews progress against material ESG issues and ensures our ESG agenda keeps pace with evolving global standards, stakeholder expectations, and regulatory requirements. The Committee meets twice a year, and its agenda directly shapes the priorities of the HSES Management Committee, the Communities of Practice, and BU-level implementation plans for the period ahead.P . Management level:  
Three parallel streams
At the executive level, three entities 
work in coordination to bridge strategy and execution, providing monthly updates and ensuring alignment with business priorities.
The HSE & Sustainability (HSES) 
Executive Committee,  operating as 
part of the Group Ex-Co, convenes monthly to update Group leadership on overall ESG progress. The ESG team directs initiatives under this committee, collaborating with internal and external stakeholders to ensure strategic priorities are translated into action.
The HSES Management Committee 
meets monthly for programme updates across all nine Aims at both Group-level and BU targets against actual progress, managing key decisions on strategic direction and cross-functional support.Vedanta Sustainability 
Framework
The Vedanta Sustainability 
Framework (VSF) serves as the foundation for integrating sustainability into our business operations and decision-making processes. It ensures that we generate positive impacts across our entire value chain while maintaining operational excellence, aligned with globally recognised standards established by the International Council on Mining and Metals (ICMM), International Finance 
Vedanta Sustainability 
Assurance Process (VSAP)
The Vedanta Sustainability Assurance 
Process (VSAP) is our primary internal audit mechanism for ensuring the effective implementation of the Vedanta Sustainability Framework across all business units. It functions as a structured performance monitoring and risk management tool, enabling the Group to assess ESG compliance and track progress across critical sustainability parameters.
Through systematic evaluation of 
environmental management, health and safety, community engagement, and human rights, VSAP identifies performance gaps and facilitates timely corrective action plans with continuous evaluation to strengthen overall sustainability outcomes. The programme operates through a structured annual cycle of internal assessments, continuous monitoring, and periodic validation by subject matter experts. Findings are reviewed by the Sustainability and Executive Committees and reported to the Board, ensuring strong governance and accountability at the highest level.
To reinforce leadership ownership 
of sustainability priorities, ESG parameters assessed through VSAP are embedded into leadership performance metrics, with sustainability criteria carrying a 15% weighting in annual performance-linked KPIs that influence executive compensation. By linking assurance, accountability, and performance, VSAP plays a critical role in driving consistent progress toward sustainability across the organisation.Level Level Level
1 2 3Vedanta Sustainability Framework – Three-Level Policy Architecture
Aligned with ICMM • IFC • OECD • UNGC • UN SDGs Overseen by EXCO monitoring mechanismCorporation (IFC), the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), United Nations Global Compact (UNGC), and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).
The VSF is supported by a three-level 
architecture of policies, standards, and guidance documents that are regularly reviewed and monitored to ensure alignment with evolving global expectations.
Through the VSF, we provide 
education, training, and capacity-building opportunities for employees and business partners to strengthen their understanding of and ability to implement sustainability principles. To read more about our policies, standards, and guidance notes, please visit our website: Link.
The VSF establishes what we are committed to and how we manage it. The Vedanta Sustainability Assurance Programme then verifies that those commitments are being honoured across all business units and geographies.Operational integration: BU 
and SBU Level
At the BU and SBU levels, dedicated 
ESG teams manage on-ground implementation, translating Group-level commitments into site -specific actions 
that are stress-tested against real world conditions, including resource constraints, community dynamics, and production realities.
Embedded Accountability
ESG ownership at this level is both structured and distributed. Dedicated BU ESG teams ensure sustainability is embedded within core operational decision-making, with ESG performance metrics sitting alongside production, safety, and financial KPIs in routine management reviews, reinforcing a culture where environmental and social considerations carry equal weight to operational targets.Community-Led ESG Delivery
Communities of Practice bring together 
representatives from multiple functions to oversee community-focussed initiatives, ensuring strong social performance by addressing stakeholder concerns and fostering meaningful engagement. By anchoring expertise within practitioner communities rather than relying solely on top-down directives, Vedanta builds institutional knowledge that is resilient, transferable, and deeply contextual, accelerating problem-solving and reducing duplication of effort across sites.
Together, these mechanisms strengthen 
Vedanta’s social licence to operate and align its actions with global sustainability standards, ensuring ESG ambitions are not confined to policy documents but are implemented, tracked, and measured daily across its diverse operational portfolio. In FY 2025-26, our CoPs conducted over 250 meetings, each a structured forum where site-level practitioners, functional experts, and BU ESG leads align on progress, resolve implementation barriers, and share innovations across the organisation.

TRANSFORMING COMMUNITIES
Keeping people and communities at the centre of our business decisions
The resources we develop are deeply 
connected to the well-being and progress of the communities around our operations. We earn our social licence to operate through consistent action, transparent engagement and commitment to shared prosperity for the local communities, stakeholders, and society.Every site maintains structured community engagement processes, grievance redressal mechanisms, and social performance teams whose mandate is to ensure our presence creates more value than it consumes. Earning our place, every day
For Vedanta, with operations spanning 
some of India's most resource-rich and community-sensitive geographies, natural resource extraction and community well-being are deeply interdependent. Vedanta creates shared benefits through transparent engagement, responsive grievance resolution, local economic participation and community-led developmental initiatives, enabling communities to grow and prosper alongside our operations.
Our three-pronged social strategy, “Do 
No Harm, Building Trust, and Benefit Sharing”, provides the operating logic through which we pursue this. Do No Harm addresses the environmental, safety, and land-related impacts of our presence at source. Building Trust is maintained through continuous, transparent dialogue and grievance mechanisms that communities can use, are accessible in local languages, and are resolved with accountability. Benefit Sharing ensures that the economic value generated by our operations flows back into host communities through local employment, local procurement, and development programmes designed around what communities need rather than what is convenient to deliver.
Engaging Responsibly with 
Indigenous Communities
We deeply acknowledge our 
responsibilities where our operations bring us into contact with indigenous peoples and tribal communities. We seek informed consent before any project that may affect indigenous lands or resources, and approach land acquisition and resettlement with legal compliance and community consultation as non-negotiable conditions.
The Kalahandi transformation story: 
A model for inclusive development
Kalahandi stands as a powerful 
example of how sustained investments, integrated development approach can drive inclusive development.Once defined by poverty, with per capita income barely touching ₹ 19,000 and contributing less than 1% to Odisha's GDP , the district now ranks first in Odisha in Health and Nutrition and second in Education under NITI Aayog's Aspirational Districts programme. Between 2003 and 2015, its GDDP grew over 16%, more than double the state average.
This transformation has been enabled 
through several systemic interventions, which included:
 Education through DAV Vedanta International School, where 83% of over 1,300 students come from tribal communities

 We also conducted Human Rights Risk Assessment (HRRA) across 100% of Vedanta’s operations through independent third-party assessment. Business Unit
Vedanta Aluminium LimitedPresence over 
programme: Employees take community commitment beyond the workplace
Impact on Vedanta
When 1,800 employees step 
outside their workplaces to serve the communities surrounding them, volunteerism stops being a programme and becomes a culture. For Vedanta Aluminium, this initiative demonstrates that social licence is not managed from a CSR department; it is carried by the people who work there every day.
What does this project do?
On International Volunteer Day 2025, Vedanta Aluminium mobilised employees across its operational facilities to lead community facing initiatives spanning healthcare, education, livelihoods, environment, and women’s empowerment, contributing 4,000 hours of service, equivalent to nearly 167 continuous days of community engagement, and reaching over 0.7 million lives across three states.exhibitions. Health camps across both states delivered preventive care to underserved communities. In Visakhapatnam, volunteers supported the establishment of digital learning labs in schools, expanding access to technology-enabled education beyond existing curricula.
Why is this project important?
Employee-led volunteerism addresses the gap between industrial presence and community opportunity differently from institutional CSR. It creates personal accountability, builds authentic relationships, and signals to communities that commitment is human and present, not distant and transactional. Embedding volunteerism into employee identity produces sustained engagement rather than episodic goodwill, and the multiplier effect compounds over time.
How is it being implemented?
The initiative was structured as a coordinated single day mobilisation across Odisha, Chhattisgarh, and Andhra Pradesh simultaneously, with each facility organising locally relevant activities rather than applying a uniform template. In Lanjigarh, volunteers supported grassroots archery development and the revival of Saura and Dokra art forms, connecting artisans to new markets while preserving cultural heritage. In Korba, employee support helped women trained through livelihood programmes showcase their enterprises at regional Outcome for stakeholders

Case Study Social Performance and 
Steering Committee (SPSC)
Composition
Each SPSC is chaired by the respective 
Business Unit CEO or an appointed site head. The on-site staff includes the Social Performance Manager, Grievance Mechanism Cells, and Community Liaison Officer. The cross-functional team draws representatives from External Affairs, Public Relations, Operations, Security, CSR, Human Resources, HSE, Finance, and Corporate Communications.Oversight and implementation 
of social performance
We follow a top-down approach 
of oversight and implementation of social performance. Implementation of the social strategy is overseen by the Business Unit CEO, with guidance from the SPSC at each site. The SPM is responsible for the on-the-ground execution of the strategy. The SPSCs, alongside the SPM and Grievance Mechanism Cells, play a critical role in fostering strong community relationships and ensuring the effective management of social performance.
We align with global human 
rights frameworks and embed these principles in our daily operations, treating freedom of association, collective bargaining, and indigenous autonomy as non-negotiable. Our grievance redressal mechanism is accessible in local languages and formats to ensure fair and fast resolution of issues. Feedback loops are integrated to strengthen continuous improvement. We also address complex issues like land acquisition and resettlement with sensitivity and legal compliance, always prioritising community consent and long-term restoration.

From skills to sustainable

Our operations span some of India's most remote and ecologically sensitive geographies, regions where access to quality education, vocational training, and formal employment has historically been limited. This is precisely where our responsibility is greatest, and where the opportunity for lasting impact is most real. that lasting transformation begins when people are empowered to shape their own futures. Our goal of empowering 2.5 million individuals with enhanced skillsets by FY 2029-30 is being delivered through community-centric, locally calibrated interventions in vocational training, entrepreneurship development, sports, and livelihood support, creating pathways to economic participation, self-reliance and sustainable prosperity.

Sports as a catalyst for social 
transformation and inclusion
Vedanta's investment in grassroots 
sports goes beyond infrastructure. In rural and tribal communities, sport is a vehicle for inclusion, identity, and economic opportunity. Our programmes span archery, football, karate, and traditional disciplines, with women-centric coaching centres created specifically to challenge the social norms that keep women off competitive pathways. We have made the inclusion of differently abled athletes a non-negotiable design principle, ensuring our sports programmes reflect the same diversity commitments we uphold across the rest of our operations.
Sports not only promote mental and 
physical well-being but also inspire discipline and unity, offering youth a pathway to national platforms and amplifying their potential. The revival of traditional sports forms part of our cultural preservation commitment, keeping indigenous heritage alive while simultaneously building community cohesion. Vedanta Sesa GoaStrengthening 
community livelihoods through the Alternate Livelihood Opportunity Project (ALOP)
Impact on Vedanta
The initiative reinforces 
Vedanta’s commitment to placing community welfare at the centre of its business decisions by supporting sustainable livelihood opportunities for local farmers. By enabling agricultural capability building and income diversification, the programme strengthens community trust, deepens local partnerships, and contributes to maintaining Vedanta’s social licence to operate.
What does this project do?
The Alternate Livelihood Opportunity Project (ALOP) focusses on creating sustainable livelihood avenues for rural communities through orchard-based farming under the Wadi model. The initiative supports small and marginal farmers by promoting fruit cultivation and providing access to high-quality saplings, technical guidance, and agricultural training. Through this intervention, farmers are encouraged to adopt diversified and sustainable farming practices that enhance productivity and income potential. Approximately, 47 acres of land have been brought under fruit cultivation through the initiative
 The programme focusses on small and marginal farmers, supporting them in adopting improved agricultural practices and building capabilities in horticulture management
Alongside plantation support, farmers receive guidance on cultivation techniques, orchard management, and sustainable agricultural practices to ensure long-term productivity and income generation.
Outcome for stakeholders
 Strengthened livelihood opportunities for small and marginal farmers through diversified agricultural practices
 Improved agricultural capabilities and adoption of horticulture-based farming systems
 Enhanced long-term income potential through fruit cultivation
 Stronger community partnerships through initiatives that place community welfare at the centre of development effortsWhy is this project important?
Agriculture remains the primary source of livelihood for many rural households; however, limited landholding sizes and low crop productivity often restrict income opportunities. By introducing horticulture-based farming systems and strengthening agricultural capabilities, the initiative enables farmers to build more resilient and sustainable livelihoods. The programme also reflects a broader approach of integrating community welfare considerations into operational decisions by supporting long-term socio-economic development in neighbouring regions.
How is it being implemented?
Vedanta Sesa Goa has implemented the initiative in villages in Karnataka through its ALOP programme, working closely with local communities and development partners. The project promotes orchard development by distributing Alphonso mango grafts and supporting farmers in establishing fruit plantations on their land.

Strengthening foundations for 
inclusive well-being
The communities that host our operations are home to some of India's most underserved populations: rural mothers with limited access to healthcare, children whose foundational years unfold in under-resourced Anganwadis, and women whose economic potential is constrained not by capability but by circumstance. We are committed to addressing these challenges through scalable, community-focussed interventions.
Our Aim 3, that seeks to uplift 100 
million women and children, is delivered through two integrated programme pillars: Nand Ghar, our 
flagship initiative modernising India's Anganwadi network since 2015; and a portfolio of women's empowerment 
programmes, including Sakhi, Unnati, 
and Subhalaxmi , that build the 
financial, social, and entrepreneurial capabilities of rural women across our operational geographies.Nand Ghar: Reimagining rural 
childhood
Nand Ghar was born of a conviction 
that the Anganwadi system, which reaches India's most vulnerable children and mothers, deserved infrastructure and resources befitting its role. Launched in collaboration with the Ministry of Women and Child Development and local NGOs, Nand Ghar modernises India's existing Anganwadi infrastructure, transforming it into vibrant centres of community development. We did not build a parallel system. We invested in transforming the existing one. Every Nand Ghar centre we establish brings solar power, safe drinking water, clean sanitation, e-learning technology, and nutritious meals to communities where these were previously unavailable. Each centre operates on a dual-shift model: mornings provide pre-school education for children aged three to six through e-learning modules, play-based learning, and nutritious meals; afternoons serve as skill development and entrepreneurship centres for women. The same building serves two generations.
Today, over 12,769 Nand Ghars are 
operational across 17 states, with an MOU signed with the Government of Rajasthan to develop 25,000 centres across the state alone. We are currently reaching 0.89 million children and women, progress towards our mission of transforming the lives of 90 million children and women across India's 1.37 million Anganwadis. Project Balvardhan in Rajasthan is addressing malnutrition at scale, currently supporting over 80,000 children and mothers in aspirational districts.
During Poshan Maah 2025, we 
engaged over 0.35 million families across 15 states under the theme "Poshan Se Pragati", combining recipe demonstrations, parent training sessions, and community awareness campaigns designed to embed

Community Engagement and Development
Business Unit
Hindustan Zinc Limited (HZL)Sakhi: Turning Self-Help into economic power
Impact on Vedanta
Sakhi has grown from a self-help group formation programme into one of India’s most substantive corporate led women’s economic empowerment initiatives. For Hindustan Zinc, operating across Rajasthan’s mining belt where women have historically been excluded from formal financial systems, the scale of credit now flowing through Sakhi’s network, and the depth of enterprise formation it has enabled, position this programme as a measurable contributor to Vedanta’s ESG commitments on gender inclusion and community development.
What does this project do?
Sakhi organises rural women into Self Help Groups, builds federations that give those groups institutional weight, and connects them to formal financial systems, enterprise opportunities, and markets. The programme spans financial literacy, microenterprise development, digital skilling, and social awareness, structured to move women from savings discipline through to credit access and independent income generation.Enterprise development support has produced tangible ownership milestones, including a women operated BPCL petrol pump in Rajasthan. Sakhi Utsav 2025 brought over 7,000 women across five districts together, a convergence of enterprise showcasing, federation strengthening, and peer learning that reflects the programme’s scale and the depth of participation it has built.
Outcome for stakeholders
 ₹ 1,490 million in credit mobilised in FY 2025-26, giving women in rural Rajasthan access to formal financial capital at a scale that enables real enterprise formation
 25,530 women organised across active Self Help Groups
 ₹ 277 million in cumulative savings and interest generated across the network
 Women-led enterprises sustained beyond initial formation, with verified income generation across member households
 Social change programming reaching communities on issues that constrain women’s economic participation at the household levelWhy is this project important?
Rural women in Rajasthan’s mining districts face compounded barriers: limited banking infrastructure, social norms that restrict financial decision-making, and no formal pathway from household savings to enterprise credit. Sakhi dismantles each barrier systematically, through institutional structures that give women financial identity, credit history, and the peer and federation support to sustain enterprises over time. Economic empowerment and social change are treated as inseparable: the Uthori theatre group runs community awareness programming on female foeticide, domestic abuse, and child marriage alongside the financial programme, recognising that income independence alone does not produce lasting transformation.
How is it being implemented?
Sakhi operates through a federated SHG architecture across 200+ village organisations, with group-level savings and governance feeding into cluster federations that interface with banks and India Post Payments Bank, giving members access to credit, insurance, and digital payment infrastructure.
Digital Sakhis, trained as community 
level financial service points, extend this reach into villages where formal banking remains distant.
Why is this project important?
Access to quality education plays a critical role in shaping the future of children and strengthening long-term community well-being. Many students in rural communities face barriers such as limited educational resources and inadequate learning support. By providing structured academic support, essential learning materials, and opportunities for holistic development, the initiative contributes to improving learning continuity and educational outcomes for children.
How is it being implemented?
The initiative is implemented through a combination of institutional education support and targeted student-focussed programmes. Two community schools are supported under the project, along with remedial coaching classes that help students strengthen their academic foundations and address learning gaps.
In addition to classroom support, the 
programme provides Teaching and Learning Materials (TLM), school uniforms, shoes, and other essential educational resources. Students Outcome for stakeholders

TRANSFORMING THE PLANET
Embedding environmental responsibility into our business model
The scale of what we do and the environmental footprint it carries are not things we describe in the abstract. 
It is the operational reality from which our environmental commitments are built, and it is the reason those commitments must be specific, time-bound, and backed by capital r ather than language. The metals we produce 
are essential to the global clean energy transition: aluminium for electric vehicles and solar panels, zinc for galvanised infrastructure, copper for transmission networks, and silver for solar technologies. This creates a fundamental tension; industries that supply materials for a greener economy must also decarbonise, conserve water, and manage waste responsibly. We address this challenge directly through clearly defined targets, committed capital, and the operational programmes.Decarbonisation
We are committed to net zero carbon emissions (Scope 1 and Scope 2) by 2050 or sooner, with 1.9 GW of installed renewable energy capacity. Power Delivery Agreements are already in place, 28 million tonnes of carbon mitigated over the last five years, and US$ 5 billion committed to the transition.

Shaping a low-carbon future
As India races to become one of the world's fastest-growing major economies, our growth will have to be low-carbon driven. As the country's premier metals and mining company, with a portfolio of nine transition metals that will play a significant role in India's green transition, we are committed to driving a low-carbon growth responsibly and by example. Our strategic pathway is aligned with India's Panchamrit commitments announced at COP26, including the ambitious national goals of reaching 500 GW of non-fossil energy capacity by 2030 and achieving net zero emissions by 2070. By aligning our near-term actions with these national objectives, we are contributing meaningfully to India's broader climate goals and the transition to a sustainable future.
Our Net Zero ambition reflects a clear 
responsibility: to lower the carbon footprint of our operations while continuing to supply the materials that power the energy transition. We pursue this through a structured, four-phase roadmap spanning FY 2021-25, FY 2021-30, FY 2026-30, and Beyond 2030, supported by US$ 5 billion of allocated capital to drive delivery at scale. Each of this phase is advancing our decarbonisation agenda through four levers:
 Increasing renewable energy
 Switching to low carbon fuels
 Improving energy and process efficiency
 Offsetting residual emissions
Each of these levers is already operational, with defined milestones for every phase.
Advancing renewable 
energy adoption
Renewable energy is our 
primary and most consequential decarbonisation lever. We have signed 1.03 GW of round-the-clock (RE-RTC) renewable energy power delivery agreements (PDAs), with construction currently underway and partial commissioning achieved on some projects. We remain on track to achieve 2.5 GW of round-the-clock equivalent non-fossil fuel-based electricity by FY 2029-30.Switching to low-carbon fuels
Fuel switching is already delivering tangible results at scale. At TSPL, we have utilised approximately 0.36 million tonnes of biomass pellets to replace around 5% of coal consumption in our thermal power operations. This intervention not only supports a meaningful shift away from fossil fuels but also delivers strong co-benefits, most notably helping address the regional stubble burning challenge by creating a viable end-use for agricultural residue.In FY 2025-26, we utilised more than 3.80 billion units of clean energy from renewable electricity and Waste Heat Recovery Boiler across our operations, achieving a ~14% reduction in emissions intensity (tCO
2e/MT) against 
our FY 2020-21 baseline, proof that the investment is translating into measured outcomes, not just stated ambition.
Targeted fuel substitution initiative has enabled the mitigation of approximately 0.4-0.5 million tonnes of CO₂ emissions, driving decarbonisation, air quality improvement, and shared value creation across the energy–agriculture nexus.Improving energy efficiency
Continuous process optimisation, digital interventions, and the adoption of best-available technologies are driving measurable improvements in energy consumption and emissions intensity across our smelting, refining, and extraction operations. Each percentage-point reduction in specific energy consumption across our aluminium, zinc, and copper businesses translates into meaningful reductions in emissions intensity at the scale at which we operate.
Our aluminium operations at Lanjigarh 
and Jharsuguda were recognised at the 26

The path forward: Hydrogen
Vedanta recognises hydrogen as a potential long-term lever for deep decarbonisation in energy-intensive operations. However, given the current state of the hydrogen economy, where infrastructure, supply chains, and cost structures remain at an early stage of maturity, work on the hydrogen transition has been paused while we monitor how the ecosystem evolves. This reflects our recognition that deep decarbonisation in energy-intensive industries will ultimately require solutions beyond renewable electricity alone.
We will revisit our hydrogen pathway 
as the economics and enabling infrastructure develop to a point where meaningful, scalable adoption becomes viable across our operations.

Vedanta Aluminium LimitedPrecision Thermal Management for Energy-Efficient Aluminium Smelting
Impact on Vedanta
Vedanta Aluminium's in-house-developed Forced Cooling Network (FCN), built on 3D Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) modelling, delivers precise sidewall temperature control across aluminium reduction cells at Jharsuguda — enabling stable, high-amperage operations and lower GHG emissions. Recognised with a Certificate of Merit at the National Energy Conservation Awards 2025, it sets a new benchmark for sustainable aluminium smelting in India.
What does this project do?
The FCN replaces conventional compressed-air cooling with a CFD-optimised system that uses digital replicas of pot structures, cooling ducts, and airflow pathways. It prevents overheating, maintains protective ledge layers, and supports stable high-current operations, reducing energy loss and enhancing overall potline reliability.Case Study 
Materiality relevancy
Climate Change and Energy Transition 
Business Unit
Hindustan Zinc LimitedDecarbonising the Last Mile — EV and LNG Trucks
Impact on Vedanta
Deepening the strategic partnership with GreenLine Mobility to deploy electric and LNG trucks at scale accelerates Hindustan Zinc's supply chain decarbonisation, directly reducing Scope 3 emissions across logistics. The ₹ 400 crore investment by GreenLine demonstrates the commercial viability of clean freight at an industrial scale, advancing Vedanta's net zero trajectory while reinforcing its position as a sustainability leader in the global metals and mining sector.
What does this project do?
The initiative deploys 100 electric trucks for inter-unit concentrate movement between mines and smelters, supported by India's first commercial-scale battery-swapping infrastructure with three high-capacity stations for 24×7 operations, alongside 100 new LNG trucks that double Hindustan Zinc's existing LNG fleet to 200 vehicles for long-haul finished-goods transport.Why is this project important?
Supply chain logistics remain a significant source of Scope 3 emissions in mining and metals operations. Transitioning to electric and LNG freight at this scale directly addresses long-haul and inter-unit carbon intensity, while battery swapping infrastructure eliminates the downtime constraints of conventional EV charging, making clean logistics operationally viable and commercially scalable for heavy industrial use.
How is it being implemented?
Formalised on 4 August 2025, the expanded partnership with GreenLine Mobility Solutions Ltd. (an Essar venture) involves deploying 100 electric trucks, manufactured by Blue Energy Motors, to replace diesel trucks for transporting concentrated materials between Hindustan Zinc's mines and smelters. Three high-capacity battery swapping stations have been established to enable continuous 24×7 operations. Simultaneously, 100 new LNG trucks have been added, doubling the fleet to 200 vehicles for long-haul transport of finished goods, significantly reducing emissions on long-distance routes.
Case Study Why is this project important?
Increasing production volumes and higher operating currents demand better thermal management. Conventional cooling systems cause pressure drops and process disruptions, directly undermining efficiency and reliability in one of the world's most energy-intensive industries. The FCN eliminates these structural inefficiencies through digital precision engineering, making potline cooling a scalable lever for industrial decarbonisation.
How is it being implemented?
Developed entirely in-house, CFD simulations optimise heat dissipation before physical deployment. Commenced on 16 July 2025 with a capital investment of ₹ 13.95 crore per potline, the FCN is being deployed in a phased approach with gradual integration into existing potroom infrastructure. Commissioned on a section of a potline at Jharsuguda, the initiative is currently 25% complete, with full impact realisation targeted by 16 July 2026. Continuous monitoring of shell temperatures ensures optimal balance throughout integration, with scale-up across the full potline to follow.Outcome for stakeholders

Hindustan Zinc LimitedAdvancing water positivity through Zero Liquid Discharge
Impact on Vedanta

What does this project do?
The project implements Zero Liquid Discharge (ZLD) systems to eliminate liquid waste discharge while maximising water recovery and reuse within operations.Why is this project important?
Given that operations are in water-constrained regions, minimising freshwater intake and preventing wastewater discharge are critical for ensuring long-term operational stability and responsible resource use.
How is it being implemented?
Hindustan Zinc Limited (HZL) has adopted the ZLD principle across all operational sites in a phased approach. In FY 2023-24 and FY 2024-25, HZL commissioned Phase 1 ZLD plants at Rampura Agucha Mine and Zawar Mines, with a combined capacity of 4,000 KLD. The system integrates Effluent Treatment Plants, Reverse Osmosis, Multiple Effect Evaporators, and Mechanical Vapour Recompression, cutting-edge technologies that collectively deliver an internal recycling capacity of 31,300 KLD across facilities.

Greener practices, stronger 
performance
The metals and mining sector carries a unique environmental obligation, not just to reduce what it extracts from the earth, but also to manage the resulting impacts with discipline and accountability. Every tonne of metal we produce generates by-products that must be handled responsibly, emissions that must be monitored and minimised, tailings that must be stored safely, and land whose biodiversity must be protected and restored. Aim 6 addresses all these dimensions through continuous improvement, innovation, and governance that holds us accountable at every level.
Advanced monitoring systems 
ensure the safety and integrity of tailings facilities, while biodiversity is safeguarded through a “Do No Harm” approach aligned with global standards to minimise environmental impact. This is reinforced by our Resource Use and Waste Management Technical Standard, which prioritises reduction and avoidance at source, followed by recovery and recycling, with disposal treated strictly as a last resort. Together, these measures support our long-term ambition of achieving 100% utilisation of hazardous and high-volume, low-toxicity waste by 2035.
These efforts are managed as part 
of an integrated system rather than isolated initiatives. Advancing circularity in waste streams improves resource efficiency and supports cost optimisation. Robust tailings management safeguards operational continuity and mitigates risk. Investments in biodiversity protection and restoration contribute to stronger community relationships and long-term site viability. Together, these actions reflect a cohesive approach to environmental management, where operational performance and responsible practices are closely aligned.
Waste to wealth: Turning by-
products into resources
Vedanta has established a Group-
wide Waste to Wealth programme that converts industrial by-products into commercially viable resources, advancing circularity across all operations. The programme is built on the principle that waste generated at one point in the value chain is a resource for another, and Vedanta's scale creates the opportunity to demonstrate that principle at a national level.
Fly ash management
Since March 2022, Vedanta Aluminium has redirected over 1.5 million tonnes of fly ash to cement manufacturers, 3 million tonnes to National Highways Authority of India highway projects, and 0.3 million tonnes to MSME brick manufacturers in Odisha and Chhattisgarh. At Lanjigarh, more than 90% of fly ash generated is utilised by local entrepreneurs, supporting regional enterprise development.
In FY 2025-26, Vedanta achieved 
101% ash utilisation across thermal power operations. Through partnerships with NHAI, CSIR, and IIT Kharagpur, Vedanta is exploring high-volume, low-toxicity waste as a sustainable road construction material, integrating circularity directly into national infrastructure development.
Metal recovery from jarosite 
residues
Vedanta has invested in advanced 
metallurgical recovery technologies across its smelting operations to close material loops on residues previously treated as process waste. At Hindustan Zinc's Chanderiya smelter, the Zinc Fumer Plant recovers zinc, lead, and silver directly from jarosite residues using high-temperature fuming technology, with the remaining slag fully utilised by the cement industry, achieving near-zero waste from this stream. The plant recovers approximately 3,000 MT of zinc, 4,700 MT of lead, and 33 MT of silver annually, while reducing jarosite by approximately 40,000 MT and saving approximately 4 hectares of landfill per year. Jarosite is further stabilised into Jarofix through lime and cement treatment, then supplied for use in road embankments, railway construction, and cement manufacturing.

by design
Tailings management is a priority 
across all our operations. Vedanta aligns its tailings governance with the Global Industry Standard on Tailings Management (GISTM), the most rigorous international benchmark for tailings facility design, operation, and closure, developed by the International Council on Mining and Metals (ICMM), the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), and the Principles for Responsible Investment (PRI). The GISTM establishes requirements across the full lifecycle of a tailings facility, from siting and design through to operation, monitoring, and long-term closure planning, with particular emphasis on protecting human life, minimising environmental impact, and ensuring transparent governance and community engagement.

Hindustan Zinc LimitedClosing the loop on legacy waste: Tailings management programme
Impact on Vedanta
HZL 's tailings management programme addresses mining's most significant long-term environmental liability while simultaneously converting legacy waste into recoverable resources. By deploying Dry Tailings technology, progressing India's first Zinc Tailings Reprocessing Plant, and repurposing tailings as underground mine backfill, HZL demonstrates how advanced waste management can reduce environmental risk, eliminate historical liabilities, and generate economic value directly supporting Vedanta's circular economy commitments and GISTM-aligned tailings governance.What does this project do?
The programme operates across 
three integrated interventions:
 Dry Tailings Technology at Zawar and Rajpura Dariba recovers more than 80% of process water from tailings slurry for operational reuse, produces compact dry-stack filter cake suitable for safe storage or backfill, and significantly reduces dam failure risk and freshwater consumption
 Underground Mine Backfill repurposes tailings and waste rock as structural fill in underground workings, reinforcing mine stability while eliminating the need for surface storage of this material
 Zinc Tailings Reprocessing Plant (10 MTPA): Board-approved 
and in advanced engineering is India's first such facility, designed to process approximately 86 million tonnes of legacy tailings and recover over 860 kt of zinc, converting decades of accumulated waste into a commercially viable resource. Engineering is progressing through design optimisation with Sedgman and Fraser Alexander, with equipment procurement and site mobilisation underway.
Why is this project important?
Legacy tailings carry persistent environmental risk and long-term financial liability. At the same time, they contain recoverable metals with significant economic value. HZL 's programme addresses both simultaneously reducing the structural risk of existing tailings facilities, eliminating ongoing wet deposition, and unlocking 860 kt of zinc from 86 million tonnes of historical waste. Advancing workplace safety 
and health
In mining and metals operations, 
safety is not a compliance requirement; it is the clearest reflection of how we value our people. Our Zero Harm vision serves as the guiding principle for how we design systems, structure governance, invest in technology, and build capability across the organisation.
Our operations carry inherent risks 
that require the highest level of safety discipline. Every fatality is preventable, and every serious incident reflects a failure of the system that allowed it to occur. This conviction drives our safety architecture, from the Board ESG Committee to the individual site safety officer.
Our framework is anchored in 
Critical Risk Management, which systematically addresses key operational risks through defined protocols and accountability mechanisms. When incidents occur, the Incident Cause Analysis Method (ICAM) drives structured investigation: identifying root causes rather than surface-level explanations and implementing targeted corrective actions to prevent recurrence. The Safety Community of Practice oversees implementation across all sites, with performance independently audited through VSAP and aligned with ISO 45001, OHSAS 18001, and International Council on Mining and Metals (ICMM) principles, reinforcing adherence to global best practices.
Our three-lever approach to safety
We have identified three critical focus areas to strengthen safety performance and prevent serious incidents across our operations.Technology transforming 
safety
Vedanta has made technology a 
Group-wide priority for identifying and eliminating risk at source, deploying digital tools, automation, and AI-driven systems across business units to reduce human exposure to hazardous conditions and strengthen real-time safety oversight.
Safety initiatives across 
operations in FY 2025-26

 Smoke-hours drilling technology in Rampura Agucha allows safe production during transition periods.
 Collision avoidance systems  are 
being deployed by Vedanta across underground mines, in partnership with Epiroc, to mitigate equipment-related risks.

Health and well-being
Our commitment to workforce well-being extends across both physical and mental health. Mantra Care, Vedanta's comprehensive employee wellness programme, provides 24/7 access to mental health counselling, therapy, and meditation, alongside resources for physical health and financial well-being through a dedicated platform. The VLL Mental Health Programme 
further integrates psychological well-being into the occupational health framework through preventive medical examinations, structured awareness initiatives, and targeted health interventions. This reflects our recognition that a safe workforce is not only protected from physical harm but also supported in maintaining mental and emotional well-being.
Structured incident 
investigation: the ICAM approach
Learning from incidents is as 
important as preventing them. Vedanta adopts the Incident Cause Analysis Method (ICAM) as its standard framework for investigating health and safety incidents across all operations. ICAM is a structured methodology that goes beyond surface-level explanations to systematically identify the underlying and root causes of an incident examining individual actions, team and supervisory factors, work environment conditions, and organisational systems that contributed to the event.
Where a conventional investigation 
might conclude with an immediate cause, ICAM goes deeper: uncovering the latent organisational conditions that enabled the incident and prescribing corrective actions at every level of the causal chain. This enables Vedanta to refine safety protocols with precision, close systemic gaps before they produce further incidents, and embed learning permanently into operational practice rather than treating it as a post-incident formality.
Through ICAM, Vedanta reinforces its 
commitment to maintaining safety standards that meet and consistently exceed international benchmarks reflecting the organisation's broader conviction that a safer operation is not only a more responsible one, but a more productive and sustainable one for all stakeholders.

Materiality relevancy
Workplace diversity and inclusion
Business Unit
Vedanta Aluminium LimitedBreaking barriers at the helm: Vedanta Group's first all-women locomotive engine team
Impact on Vedanta
The deployment of Vedanta Group's first all-women locomotive engine team at the Jharsuguda aluminium smelter, marking a significant milestone in its inclusion agenda. By placing women at the helm of one of the plant's most critical logistical operations, Vedanta Aluminium has demonstrated that the commitment to gender equity extends to every function, including those that have historically been the most resistant to change. This initiative strengthens Vedanta's reputation as an employer of choice in the manufacturing sector, reinforces the Group's target of 30% women workforce representation by FY 2029-30, and builds the cultural credibility that attracts and retains diverse talent across all operations.
What does this project do? 
Vedanta Aluminium has deployed a dedicated all-women team to manage the locomotive engine responsible for the internal movement of raw materials at its world-class aluminium smelter in Jharsuguda, Vedanta Group's largest aluminium plant. The team comprises four loco drivers operating in shifts, one gatewoman, and two support staff, collectively responsible for the efficient and safe operation and maintenance of this critical logistics asset.Case Study This initiative is part of a broader, structured effort to open all operational roles to women across the plant. It follows a series of industry-first interventions at Jharsuguda, the launch of 'Shree Shakti', through which 108 women have taken on key operational roles during night shifts (a first in Odisha's industrial landscape), and the inauguration of the Indian aluminium industry's first all-women managed potline. The potline, a critical part of the aluminium production process, is being operationalised in three phases with more than 100 women selected through internal job postings and upskilled through specialised training programmes.
Why is this project important?
The locomotive engine function sits at the core of plant logistics, without it, the movement of raw materials that feeds the entire smelting operation would stop. Placing women in charge of this function is a deliberate operational decision that reflects Vedanta Aluminium's conviction in gender-agnostic roles. In a country where women remain significantly underrepresented in mining, metals, and manufacturing, initiatives like this reshape what is perceived as possible for the women who take on these roles, for the colleagues who work alongside them, and for the next generation of women considering industrial careers. Vedanta Aluminium's approach also directly addresses a structural talent constraint: expanding the recruitment pool to include the full workforce, not half of it, produces stronger operational outcomes and greater organisational resilience.
